variants.title: Resolve one event
variants.context: Every accepted event must resolve to one durable, reviewable outcome even when delivery repeats or compute disappears. The handler receives a versioned event, validates and atomically claims it, launches durable work, records evidence against the workflow identity, then promotes through a gate or quarantines the failure.
variants.prompt: A new dataset lands and an event triggers a retraining workflow. Put the handler stages in order.

items.text: Launch durable work by submitting preparation, training, or evaluation to compute whose lifetime and resources fit the job.
Receive a versioned event carrying a stable event ID, producer, schema version, dataset version, timestamp, and trace context.
Validate and claim it by authenticating the producer, checking the payload and policy, and atomically mapping the event ID to one workflow ID.
Record evidence by binding inputs, code, configuration, artifacts, metrics, approvals, and terminal state to the workflow identity.
Promote through the evidence gate, or route the failure to an owned recovery path.

variants.hint: The handler coordinates; it is not where the long job runs.
variants.explanation: The function finishes fast enough to retry safely, so it claims the event and starts durable work rather than doing the work itself.

variants.title: Resolve one event
variants.context: Every accepted event must resolve to one durable, reviewable outcome even when delivery repeats or compute disappears. The handler receives a versioned event, validates and atomically claims it, launches durable work, records evidence against the workflow identity, then promotes through a gate or quarantines the failure.
variants.prompt: The same event is delivered twice because the first invocation timed out after starting external work. Put what happens in order.

items.text: The atomic claim finds an existing mapping for that event ID instead of creating a new one.
The handler returns the original workflow ID rather than launching a second training job.
Evidence and terminal state continue to accumulate against that one workflow identity.
Validation passes again, since the payload and producer are unchanged.
The second delivery arrives carrying the same stable event ID.

variants.hint: At-least-once delivery is the normal case, not the exception.
variants.explanation: A durable claim stored outside ephemeral function memory is what makes repeated delivery converge on the original workflow instead of duplicating work.

variants.title: Resolve one event
variants.context: Every accepted event must resolve to one durable, reviewable outcome even when delivery repeats or compute disappears. The handler receives a versioned event, validates and atomically claims it, launches durable work, records evidence against the workflow identity, then promotes through a gate or quarantines the failure.
variants.prompt: An event fails schema validation on every attempt. Put the handling steps in order.

items.text: The quarantined event is attached to a named owner with its failure reason and trace context.
It re-enters production only through an explicit, reviewed replay rather than a blind flush.
The exhausted message is moved to the quarantine path instead of retrying forever.
The handler rejects the payload before any external side effect is started.
The attempt counter is incremented and the bounded retry budget is consumed.

variants.hint: Deterministic failures do not get better with more attempts.
variants.explanation: Poison events are quarantined with an owner and an explicit replay process, because replaying dead letters blindly reintroduces the same failure.

variants.title: Release with evidence
variants.context: A model release moves through four stages. Build pins the source revision, locks, image, feature contract, and configuration. Evaluate runs quality, fairness, safety, latency, cold-start, memory, and cost checks. Promote records a policy decision against one immutable artifact. Recover retains the previous artifact and proves replay is safe.
variants.prompt: A candidate model is ready to reach production through the serverless path. Put the release stages in order.

items.text: Promote: record the policy decision against one immutable artifact and compare a canary or shadow revision with the baseline.
Evaluate: run data-quality, model-quality, fairness, safety, latency, cold-start, memory, and cost checks against explicit thresholds.
Build: pin the source revision, dependency lock, runtime image, feature contract, and training configuration, then emit provenance.
Recover: retain the previous artifact and configuration, define automated rollback signals, and prove replay does not create a second workflow.

variants.hint: Each stage produces the evidence the next stage decides on.
variants.explanation: Promotion binds a decision to one immutable artifact, which is why mutable object paths and image tags cannot serve as model identity.

variants.title: Release with evidence
variants.context: A model release moves through four stages. Build pins the source revision, locks, image, feature contract, and configuration. Evaluate runs quality, fairness, safety, latency, cold-start, memory, and cost checks. Promote records a policy decision against one immutable artifact. Recover retains the previous artifact and proves replay is safe.
variants.prompt: A team wants proof that this release can be reversed before it takes traffic. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Replay a delivered event and verify it maps to the existing workflow rather than a new one.
Pin and scan the artifact so the exact bytes being promoted are identified.
Measure cold-start, memory, and cost alongside quality so the recovery target is comparable.
Confirm the previous artifact and its configuration are still retained and deployable.
Deploy the candidate as a shadow or canary revision beside the current baseline.

variants.explanation: Recovery is a release stage in its own right, so the retained artifact and a proven replay path exist before exposure begins.

variants.title: Release with evidence
variants.context: A model release moves through four stages. Build pins the source revision, locks, image, feature contract, and configuration. Evaluate runs quality, fairness, safety, latency, cold-start, memory, and cost checks. Promote records a policy decision against one immutable artifact. Recover retains the previous artifact and proves replay is safe.
variants.prompt: A monitoring rule requests evaluation of a newly trained artifact. Put the path from that request to a decision in order.

items.text: The pinned artifact, its inputs, and its environment are resolved from the registry.
The results are bound to the artifact as an approval or a rejection.
The monitoring event is claimed and mapped to one workflow identity.
The evaluation suite runs against explicit thresholds rather than against the previous run's numbers.
Promotion proceeds only through the gate, and the newest artifact never ships on recency alone.

variants.hint: The newest artifact is a candidate, not a winner.
variants.explanation: A promotion gate binds inputs, code, artifact, evaluation, and approval together, which is what stops recency from acting as evidence.

variants.title: Match the execution shape
variants.context: The execution shape follows the workload contract. A synchronous function suits small artifacts and bounded work when warm and cold paths both meet the deadline. A queue-backed worker absorbs bursts when completion can be asynchronous. A durable job runs long training. A dedicated endpoint serves sustained traffic.
variants.prompt: Uploads arrive in unpredictable bursts, each needs a few seconds of scoring, and no caller waits for the result. Which shape fits?
options: A synchronous function, since each upload is small and independent.
A dedicated endpoint, since bursts imply sustained serving capacity.
A queue-backed worker, so bursts are absorbed and completion stays asynchronous.
optionFeedback: No caller is waiting, so a synchronous contract adds a deadline the workload does not have.
Bursty arrival is not sustained utilization, so a standing fleet would idle between peaks.
Correct: when completion can be asynchronous, the queue absorbs the burst and exposes age and attempts.
variants.hint: Ask whether anyone is waiting for this result right now.
variants.explanation: A queue-backed worker turns burst absorption into an explicit contract of queue age, attempt count, idempotency, dead letters, and result identity.

variants.title: Match the execution shape
variants.context: The execution shape follows the workload contract. A synchronous function suits small artifacts and bounded work when warm and cold paths both meet the deadline. A queue-backed worker absorbs bursts when completion can be asynchronous. A durable job runs long training. A dedicated endpoint serves sustained traffic.
variants.prompt: A 30 MB model does light preprocessing, and measured warm and cold paths both fit inside the caller's deadline. Which shape fits?
options: A dedicated endpoint, because any synchronous path deserves a standing fleet.
A synchronous function, with downstream connections protected from automatic concurrency.
A durable job, so the work is submitted to managed compute.
optionFeedback: A standing fleet is not required when both measured paths already meet the deadline.
Correct: small artifacts and bounded work qualify once the cold path has been measured, not assumed.
A durable job adds asynchronous coordination that a bounded, fast request does not need.
variants.hint: The cold path has to be measured before it can be called acceptable.
variants.explanation: An average latency can hide a cold tail, so warm execution and initialization are measured separately before a synchronous function is chosen.

variants.title: Match the execution shape
variants.context: The execution shape follows the workload contract. A synchronous function suits small artifacts and bounded work when warm and cold paths both meet the deadline. A queue-backed worker absorbs bursts when completion can be asynchronous. A durable job runs long training. A dedicated endpoint serves sustained traffic.
variants.prompt: Traffic is continuous all day, the artifact is several gigabytes, and the model needs an accelerator. Which shape fits?
options: A dedicated endpoint on an autoscaled serving fleet.
A synchronous function with provisioned warm instances.
A queue-backed worker that keeps the model loaded between messages.
optionFeedback: Correct: sustained utilization, large artifacts, and accelerators are exactly where a standing fleet wins.
Warming instances does not solve artifact size, accelerator need, or pay-per-use cost at continuous load.
Queueing changes when work runs, not whether the runtime can hold a multi-gigabyte accelerated model.
variants.hint: Add up what has to be resident and how often it is used.
variants.explanation: Serverless is a poor default for very large artifacts, accelerators, and sustained traffic whose pay-per-use cost exceeds a dedicated pool.

variants.title: Pick the control
variants.context: Serverless controls exist because scale-to-zero is an execution choice, not a substitute for state. Schema versions reject bad producers before side effects, idempotency claims live outside function memory, attempts and concurrency are bounded, and poison events are quarantined with an owner and a replay process.
variants.prompt: Match each control to the failure it prevents.

pairs.label: Versioned event schemas
pairs.detail: An unsupported producer causes side effects before anyone notices.

pairs.label: Idempotency claims stored outside function memory
pairs.detail: A repeated delivery launches a second training workflow.

pairs.label: Bounded attempts with a quarantine path
Concurrency capped below the downstream envelope

variants.hint: Each control answers a specific way the event path can go wrong.
variants.explanation: Scale-to-zero is an execution choice, so workflow state, idempotency, bounded attempts, and downstream limits still have to be designed.

variants.title: Pick the control
variants.context: Serverless controls exist because scale-to-zero is an execution choice, not a substitute for state. Schema versions reject bad producers before side effects, idempotency claims live outside function memory, attempts and concurrency are bounded, and poison events are quarantined with an owner and a replay process.
variants.prompt: Match each production symptom to the control that is missing.

pairs.label: Two identical training jobs started from one dataset arrival
pairs.detail: The claim was not atomic or not durable.

pairs.label: The registry runs out of connections during a traffic spike
pairs.detail: Worker concurrency was never capped below the envelope.

pairs.label: The same malformed message reappears every few minutes
pairs.detail: Attempts were unbounded and nothing was quarantined.

pairs.label: Nobody can tell which event produced a deployed model
pairs.detail: Event, workflow, artifact, and deployment identities were not correlated.

variants.hint: Read the symptom as the absence of a specific guarantee.
variants.explanation: Correlated identities across event, workflow, job, artifact, deployment, and trace are what make an incident answerable rather than reconstructed.

variants.title: Pick the control
variants.context: Serverless controls exist because scale-to-zero is an execution choice, not a substitute for state. Schema versions reject bad producers before side effects, idempotency claims live outside function memory, attempts and concurrency are bounded, and poison events are quarantined with an owner and a replay process.
variants.prompt: Match each trap to the consequence it produces.

pairs.label: Training inside a short-lived trigger
pairs.detail: The job dies at the runtime limit with no checkpoint to resume.

pairs.label: Treating scale-out as unlimited downstream capacity
pairs.detail: The dependency becomes the outage instead of the function.

pairs.label: Using a mutable object path as model identity
pairs.detail: Nobody can prove which bytes were evaluated and approved.

pairs.label: Replaying dead letters into production blindly
pairs.detail: The original failure is reintroduced at higher volume.

variants.hint: Each trap is convenient at first and expensive at the moment it matters.
variants.explanation: These traps share one cause: treating automatic scaling as a substitute for durable state, bounded limits, and immutable identity.

variants.title: Plan the capacity
variants.context: Capacity is planned before automatic scaling is trusted. Required concurrency is the arrival rate multiplied by execution seconds, cold-path latency is the sum of runtime startup, dependency import, artifact download, model load, and first execution, and worker concurrency is capped below the connection and quota envelopes.
variants.prompt: Requests arrive at 240 per second and each warm execution takes 0.25 seconds. What concurrency is required before burst and safety factors?
variants.hint: Concurrency is how much work is in flight at once.
variants.explanation: Required concurrency is arrival rate times execution seconds, which is the figure a regional quota and downstream envelope must both accommodate.

mistakes.feedback: That divides by the execution time instead of multiplying by it.
That is the arrival rate alone and ignores how long each execution holds a slot.

variants.title: Plan the capacity
variants.context: Capacity is planned before automatic scaling is trusted. Required concurrency is the arrival rate multiplied by execution seconds, cold-path latency is the sum of runtime startup, dependency import, artifact download, model load, and first execution, and worker concurrency is capped below the connection and quota envelopes.
variants.prompt: A cold invocation measures runtime startup 120 ms, dependency import 260 ms, artifact download 700 ms, model load 400 ms, and first execution 90 ms. What is the cold-path latency?
variants.hint: The cold path includes everything that happens before the caller gets an answer.
variants.explanation: Cold-path latency is the sum of startup, import, download, load, and first execution, which is why it must be measured separately from the warm path.

mistakes.feedback: That is the execution time alone, which is what a warm invocation would show.
That leaves out the first execution, which the caller also waits for.

variants.title: Plan the capacity
variants.context: Capacity is planned before automatic scaling is trusted. Required concurrency is the arrival rate multiplied by execution seconds, cold-path latency is the sum of runtime startup, dependency import, artifact download, model load, and first execution, and worker concurrency is capped below the connection and quota envelopes.
variants.prompt: A database allows 200 connections and 40 are reserved for other services. Each function instance opens 2 connections. What is the highest worker concurrency that stays inside the envelope?
variants.hint: Work backwards from what the dependency can actually accept.
variants.explanation: The cap is the connections available to this workload divided by the connections each instance opens, because concurrency must stay below the downstream envelope.

mistakes.feedback: That ignores the 40 connections reserved for other services.
That is the number of connections available, not the number of instances they support.
